import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

## The symptom

An su session ran the obvious diagnostics for "is papercusp.com down?" from
inside its own `Bash` tool and got a *unanimous, internally-consistent*
picture of total failure:

```
dig papercusp.com A @1.1.1.1     -> 18.204.152.241 (x2, duplicated in one ANSWER section)
dig www.papercusp.com A @1.1.1.1 -> 18.204.152.241 (x2)
dig papercusp.com AAAA           -> ::
curl -sv http://18.204.152.241/  -> HTTP 204, Server: nginx, ~0.5s
curl -sv https://18.204.152.241/ -> hangs, times out on :443
```

Every normal sanity control **passed and reinforced the false conclusion**:
`google.com`, `github.com`, `debian.org`, and obscure-but-real domains
(`sqlite.org`, `lwn.net`) all resolved *correctly* over the exact same path.
Querying the zone's own authoritative nameserver directly gave the *same
wrong answer*. python's `socket.getaddrinfo` agreed. The session came within
one owner approval of requesting Cloudflare dashboard access to "fix" DNS
records that were never broken — which would have **broken a healthy
production zone**.

<Aside type="danger" title="Never conclude a production outage from in-sandbox DNS alone">
If dig/curl/python inside your own Bash tool says a **workspace-owned**
domain is down, that is not sufficient evidence. Verify via a path that does
NOT share this box's network stack (below) before writing an incident report,
before proposing a DNS change, and *especially* before requesting
DNS/CDN dashboard credentials.
</Aside>

## What it actually was (verified live, 2026-07-18) — NOT a sandbox feature

The original hypothesis (filed as EI-12952) was that the **su Bash sandbox
itself synthesizes DNS answers** for non-allowlisted hosts — i.e. a designed
network-isolation feature in the agent runtime returning plausible-looking
fake records instead of failing closed. That would point the fix at
papercusp's own sandboxing code.

**Live re-investigation found a different, more mundane root cause: this
specific dev box's LAN is hijacking plain UDP port-53 answers for
`papercusp.com` (and its subdomains) to a stale/wrong IP — while TCP DNS and
any externally-routed lookup return the true answer.** This is not a
papercusp-authored sandbox behavior at all; there is no code in this repo
that implements DNS interception for the `su` Bash tool's network path (the
one adjacent mechanism, `p2p/sandbox/network-egress.ts`, is an nft
port-egress allow/denylist for **foreign P2P fleet isolation** and is not
wired into any production spawn path — unrelated).

The tell that separates "designed sandbox synthesis" from "local network
hijack" is **UDP vs TCP**:

```bash
# UDP (default) — WRONG, hijacked:
$ dig +short papercusp.com A @1.1.1.1
18.204.152.241
18.204.152.241

# TCP (bypasses the hijack) — CORRECT, matches the real Cloudflare-proxied zone:
$ dig +short +tcp papercusp.com A @1.1.1.1
172.67.145.145
104.21.73.140
```

And it is **domain-specific**, not a general TCP-vs-UDP artifact — `example.com`
and `sqlite.org` resolve identically over UDP and TCP on the same box, at the
same time:

```bash
$ dig +short example.com A @1.1.1.1        # UDP
172.66.147.243
104.20.23.154
$ dig +short +tcp example.com A @1.1.1.1   # TCP — same answer, order differs
104.20.23.154
172.66.147.243
```

Querying the LAN router directly (`@192.168.40.1`) reproduces the same wrong
answer, and a machine-local `systemd-resolved` drop-in
(`/etc/systemd/resolved.conf.d/papercusp-fallback-dns.conf`, added 2026-07-01
for an unrelated "router DNS degraded" incident) does not explain it either —
it only adds fallback servers, used when the primary is unresponsive. The
most likely explanation is a stale DNS override or security-appliance sinkhole
rule somewhere on this box's LAN, targeting `papercusp.com` specifically
(possibly a leftover from old infra pointing at a since-retired Heroku IP,
predating the current Cloudflare-fronted setup) — this is host/network
infrastructure outside papercusp's own git tree and outside this doc's scope
to fix; see "What was NOT fixed" below.

## The reliable check — verify via a path that skips this box's network entirely

**`WebFetch`** does not share the sandbox's local network stack (it fetches
server-side, via Anthropic's own infrastructure), so it is immune to a
box-local hijack by construction — not because it is "more careful" about DNS,
but because it never touches this box's compromised path at all:

```
WebFetch https://dns.google/resolve?name=<host>&type=A
```

`dig +tcp` is a fast **local corroborating signal** (works from inside the
Bash tool, no extra round-trip) but is weaker evidence than an externally-routed
check — a sufficiently capable on-path interceptor could in principle also
hijack TCP:53; the UDP-only behavior observed here is consistent with a
common, simpler class of DNS interceptor (many consumer/SMB
filtering appliances and "safe DNS" hijacks only intercept UDP:53, which is
connectionless and easy to spoof/redirect, and skip TCP:53, which requires
full connection proxying).

<Aside type="note" title="cloudflare-dns.com needs a header WebFetch can't send">
`https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query` returns HTTP 400 via `WebFetch` because
it requires an `Accept: application/dns-json` header that WebFetch does not
send. Use `https://dns.google/resolve?name=<host>&type=<A|AAAA>` instead.
</Aside>

## What to do when you see this

1. **Do not conclude an outage, and do not propose or make a DNS/CDN change**,
   on the basis of an in-sandbox measurement (`dig`, `curl`, `python
   socket.getaddrinfo`, or even querying the zone's own authoritative NS from
   inside the Bash tool) alone.
2. Cross-check with `WebFetch https://dns.google/resolve?name=<host>&type=A`
   (and `type=AAAA`). If it disagrees with your in-sandbox `dig`, the
   in-sandbox path is the one that's wrong.
3. `dig +tcp <host> @1.1.1.1` as a fast local corroborating signal — if it
   already agrees with the external check while plain UDP `dig` doesn't,
   that's the same box-local-hijack signature described here, not a fresh
   incident.
4. If the domain genuinely IS down (external check agrees with the bad
   in-sandbox reading), that's real — proceed normally.

## What was NOT fixed here (and why)

The original item's "preferred" fixes — make the sandbox's DNS layer fail
loudly instead of synthesizing, or allowlist the workspace's own domains in
the sandbox network policy — target a **designed sandbox network-isolation
feature**. Live investigation found no such feature in papercusp's own code
governing the `su` Bash tool's network path; the observed behavior is
consistent with **this specific dev box's local network** (router-level DNS
interception or a stale override), which is:

- outside papercusp's git tree (no code here implements it),
- specific to this one machine's network environment (not guaranteed to
  reproduce, or to be fixable the same way, on a different host), and
- not something an su session has the authority or the right vantage point to
  fix (it would mean reconfiguring a LAN router or an upstream network
  security appliance, not this codebase).

The durable, host-independent fix that IS in scope — and that ships alongside
this doc — is the standing habit above (verify externally before trusting an
in-sandbox DNS reading for a workspace domain) plus a small reusable, tested
pure-decider (`packages/operator-core/lib/dns-truth-divergence.ts`) any future
health check or agent tooling can call to compare an in-sandbox resolution
against an externally-supplied truth and flag exactly this divergence
pattern, instead of every agent re-deriving the UDP/TCP tell from scratch.
